headline: Brent has slid to about $91.7 as surplus expectations outweigh a fresh run of Hormuz tanker attacks, so the next 24 hours turn on whether Iran's two-day reopening plan gains traction or the attacks begin to cut physical flows.
overview: Brent is at $91.70 and WTI at $84.98, both down about 4.1% over 24 hours and down 16% and 18% respectively over 30 days. Brent closed at $95.84 on Friday and $92.44 on Monday. Reuters reported that oil settled more than 3% lower on Monday as signs of recovering Hormuz flows reinforced surplus expectations, even though fresh tanker incidents underscored risks to Middle East exports. The IEA said on Friday that the market will return to surplus in the fourth quarter as Middle East exports recover faster than demand. That surplus narrative has dominated for now, while attacks on shipping, Houthi gains in Yemen and Iranian strikes on Bahrain have not produced a lasting rally.

developments.title: Further tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz; Iran says four vessels hit mines in 24 hours
developments.summary: UKMTO reported two tanker attacks in the strait on Monday 16 November. Both caused engine-room fires and one vessel was left disabled. The later incident, at about 1900 UTC and seven nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, left the crew safe, with the extent of damage unknown. UKMTO did not identify the vessel or the attacker, and the link to Iran's mine claim has not been independently confirmed. Iran's Army said a further tanker with its navigation systems switched off struck a naval mine in a prohibited zone east of the strait. Iran described this as its fourth tanker strike in 24 hours. A tracker site, which is lower-quality evidence, cited an IMF PortWatch count of 3 transits on 8 November against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 per day.
developments.why_it_matters: The attack on a vessel in the narrowest part of the strait is the clearest threat to flows this week. The price reaction so far has been small because reported barrels lost are small and the IEA says exports are recovering, apparently through transponder-off crossings. If insurers or owners pull back from the Oman-side route, the risk premium would rebuild quickly, probably by several dollars within a session.

developments.title: IEA sees a Q4 2026 surplus; Gulf exports recovering
developments.summary: In its November report on 13 November, the IEA said Q4 supply would average 105 million bpd, 1.7 million bpd above demand, reversing its earlier forecast of a deficit. It sees 2026 demand falling 2.7 million bpd to 102.3 million bpd, then rebounding by 2 million bpd in 2027. The 2027 surplus is put at 3.8 million bpd. A further 71 million barrels of emergency stocks, including 15 million barrels of diesel, are to be made available by end-February. The agency said downside risks to its forecast persist because attacks on shipping undermine maritime security. The report is from Friday but remains the main cited driver of Tuesday's decline.
developments.why_it_matters: A balance moving from deficit to a 1.7 million bpd surplus removes the case for a sustained physical premium and shifts the focus to inventory rebuilding. The effect is persistent rather than a one-day event, but it depends on exports holding up under continued attacks.

developments.title: Houthis advance towards Aden after Saudi-backed forces leave the Bab el-Mandeb coast
developments.summary: The Yemeni government said on Sunday it was withdrawing from areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to concentrate on defending Aden. Five Yemeni military sources said on Monday that Houthi fighters had reached Khor Omairh, about 62 miles west of Aden. A maritime security assessment cited by OilPrice said Houthi control of the coast between Bab el-Mandeb and Aden would present a major increase in the threat to merchant shipping. I found no report of a new Houthi attack on a tanker in the last 24 hours.
developments.why_it_matters: The Red Sea route via Yanbu is the main Saudi alternative to Hormuz. Riyadh increasingly relies on the Bab al-Mandeb waterway for oil exports. The threat is to Saudi barrels and to a second chokepoint rather than a realised loss, so the effect stays latent unless attacks on Red Sea tankers resume.

developments.title: Iran's two-day Hormuz plan backed by regional bloc; Vance rules out a 'forever war'
developments.summary: Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi said on Monday that a 10-nation regional bloc had backed Tehran's plan to reopen Hormuz under an initial ceasefire. Tehran has demanded the release of frozen assets, sanctions relief and an end to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports in exchange. Iran said on 11 November that the strait will not reopen until the US meets its seven conditions. US Vice President Vance said in a Fox News interview that Trump would not allow the conflict to become a forever war. He did not set a withdrawal date. Araghchi is due to visit Oman on Tuesday. I found no US acceptance of the plan.
developments.why_it_matters: These are diplomatic signals with no agreed terms. They support the view that the US is looking for an exit, which trims the tail risk of renewed strikes. A formal reopening would remove the remaining Hormuz premium, but the Iranian conditions are stringent and unaccepted.

developments.title: Iranian drone strikes on Bahrain base; unverified Iranian drone claims; third US carrier arrives
developments.summary: The IRGC said its forces carried out a drone attack on a US radar system at a base in Bahrain on Sunday. Bahrain said it intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks, the first such interceptions since September. Iranian outlets also said the army shot down a US MQ-1 drone, and the IRGC said it seized a US drone near Hormuz (Iranian state-linked claims, not confirmed by the US in the material I found). CNBC's headline reports that a third US carrier has arrived, stoking concerns about renewed conflict with Iran.
developments.why_it_matters: Direct Iranian fire on US-hosted bases, plus a larger US naval presence, raises the chance of a resumption of strikes, which was the main upside risk to prices earlier this month. Markets have so far treated these as contained incidents, so the premium effect is modest unless damage or casualties follow.

developments.title: OPEC holds capacity-review meeting ahead of 29 November ministerial
developments.summary: OPEC held an online meeting on Monday to discuss its review of maximum sustainable production capacity of members and the wider OPEC+ group, according to its official X page. Secretary General Haitham Al Ghais called it a historic milestone. OPEC did not disclose specific decisions or conclusions. OPEC+ held December targets on 1 November and has about 2 million bpd of restrictions in place through end-2026 that need a decision. OPEC+ ministers will meet on 29 November to decide 2027 output policy.
developments.why_it_matters: The capacity numbers will determine how 2027 quotas are allocated, with an IEA-projected 2027 surplus of 3.8 million bpd in the background. No decision is due today, so the effect is on positioning and leaks about quota size rather than on barrels.

developments.title: US SPR falls to 276.4 million barrels, lowest since August 1982
developments.summary: Reuters reported, citing Department of Energy data, that SPR crude stocks fell to 276.4 million barrels last week, the lowest since August 1982, as part of a US agreement to release 172 million barrels. The EIA series supplied to me shows 279.5 million barrels for the week to 6 November, so the two figures are probably different weeks. The IEA's Birol is also reported (by EnergyNow, headline only) as saying a second coordinated stock release is not being discussed.
developments.why_it_matters: SPR releases are adding barrels now, which has supported the surplus narrative, but a depleted reserve leaves less of a policy backstop if Hormuz flows fall again. The latter only matters in an escalation scenario.

developments.title: China: October crude imports at seven-month high, but refinery runs fell and stockpiling resumed
developments.summary: China imported 41.94 million tonnes of crude in October (9.88 million bpd), up 9.4% per day from September, according to customs data. Refinery throughput slipped about 2% to roughly 13.7 million bpd. Reuters columnist Clyde Russell estimates that China added close to 490,000 bpd to stockpiles, reversing a September draw. Fuel exports fell to about 5.2 million tonnes from about 7.2 million in September.
developments.why_it_matters: Rising imports with falling runs means barrels are going into storage rather than being consumed, which is consistent with a looser crude balance. Lower Chinese product exports are mildly supportive of cracks.

developments.title: Product cracks compress while diesel stays the IEA's main concern
developments.summary: The dashboard shows the crack spread at $33.30 per barrel against a one-month average of $40.41, which is 3.1 standard deviations below average and down $5.05 over five days. The IEA said severe tightness in product supply, especially diesel, remains the overriding concern even as crude swings to surplus. The EIA data supplied show US distillate stocks rose 4.07 million barrels in the week to 6 November against a five-year average change of -1.69 million.
developments.why_it_matters: Falling cracks reduce the incentive for refiners to run hard and bid for crude, which weighs on crude over days. The diesel tightness flagged by the IEA suggests the crack move may overshoot, so it is a modest two-way risk.

public_sentiment.summary: Retail commentary on StockTwits is thin and tilts slightly bearish on USO, with several posters pointing to the sell-off as evidence that the earlier rally was fake. A few bullish posters cite the Gulf conflict and the SPR low. This is opinion and does not by itself confirm any development. Its mild bearish lean agrees with the price action and the IEA surplus view, but the sample is small. Reddit data was unavailable and my retail-forum search returned nothing usable.

verdict.reasoning: The strongest bearish argument is the IEA's move to a 1.7 million bpd Q4 surplus and Reuters-reported evidence that Gulf exports are recovering. The market has repeatedly sold tanker-attack headlines over the past week, and the US data show product stock builds. The strongest bullish argument is the cluster of Hormuz attacks, including one in the narrowest part of the strait, together with Houthi gains near Bab el-Mandeb and Iranian strikes on a US base. Brent's front spread of $2.45 over the second month also points to some physical tightness, and speculative positioning is at the 12th percentile of three years, which limits further liquidation. For the next 24 hours I give the edge to the bearish side, but only weakly: the price has already fallen about 4%, the dashboard rule-based signals are no-trade for Brent, and a confirmed loss of Hormuz or Red Sea flows would reverse the bias quickly.
